Surah Nuh is Meccan, and it has twenty-eight verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, [saying]: "Warn your people before a painful punishment comes to them."﴾ (71:1)

The discussion has already passed in "al-A'raf" [see vol. 7, p. 232] that Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger to be sent. Qatadah narrated it from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The first messenger to be sent was Noah, and he was sent to all the people of the earth." Therefore, when they disbelieved, Allah drowned all the people of the earth. He is Noah son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh, who is Idris, son of Yard, son of Mahla'il, son of Anush, son of Qaynan, son of Shith, son of Adam, peace be upon him. Wahb said: "They were all believers." He was sent to his people when he was fifty years old. Ibn Abbas said: he was forty years old. Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: he was sent when he was three hundred and fifty years old. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-Ankabut.

The matter concerning it is settled. And all praise is due to Allah.

(﴿that warn your people﴾) meaning: "that you warn your people." So the position of "an" is in the accusative by removing the preposition. It was also said that its position is in the genitive because of the strength of its service with "an." It is permissible for "an" to carry the meaning of the explanatory particle (al-mufassirah), in which case it has no position in grammatical analysis, because the sending carries the meaning of a command, so there is no need to assume a hidden "ba'." The reading of Abdullah is ﴿Warn your people﴾ without "an," meaning: "We said to him: warn your people." The meaning of warning has already been discussed at the beginning of "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 1, p. 184].

(﴿before a painful punishment comes to them﴾) Ibn Abbas said: it means the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. Al-Kalbi said: it is what descended upon them of the flood. It was also said: meaning, warn them of the painful punishment in general if they do not believe. He would call his people and warn them, but saw no one answering him, and they would beat him until he fainted, and he would say: "My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know." This has been discussed fully in Surat al-Ankabut [see vol. 13, p. 332]. And praise is due to Allah.

al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran* (commentary), on Surah 71, verses 2–4:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "O my people, I am to you a plain warner."﴾ That is, a frightener.

*(Mubin)*: that is, one who makes clear to you in your own tongue, which you understand.

*(An i'budu Allaha wa-ttaquhu)*: *an* here is the explanatory *an* (*al-mufassira*, the one that explains what precedes), as explained earlier concerning *an andhir*. *I'budu* means: affirm His oneness. *Wa-ttaquhu* means: fear Him.

*(Wa-ati'un)*: that is, in what I command you, for I am the messenger of Allah to you.

*(Yaghfir lakum min dhunubikum)*: *yaghfir* is in the jussive (*juzima*) as a response to the imperative. *Min* is an extra (*ziyada*) particle. The meaning of the sentence is: He will forgive you your sins. This is the view of al-Suddi. It was said: it is not correct that it is extra, because *min* is not added in an affirmative obligation; rather it is here for partition (*tab'id*), meaning some of the sins, namely those not connected with the rights of created beings. It was also said: it is to specify the kind (*bayan al-jins*). But this is remote, since no suitable kind has preceded it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is that He will bring you out of your sins (*yukhrijukum min dhunubikum*). Ibn Shajara said: the meaning is that He will forgive you those of your sins that you ask forgiveness for.

*(Wa yu'akhkhirkum ila ajalin musamma)*: Ibn Abbas said: that is, He will lengthen your lifespans (*yunsi'u fi a'marikum*). Its meaning is that Allah, before creating them, had decreed that if they believed He would bless their lifespans, and if they did not believe they would be hastened to punishment. Muqatil said: He will delay you until the end of your appointed terms in well-being, so He will not punish you with famine or other things. According to this, the meaning is that He will delay you from punishments and hardships until your appointed terms. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, He will delay you from punishment, so that you die other than the death of those who are uprooted by punishment. Accordingly, it was said: *ajalin musamma* is an appointed term known to you, by which you will not die by drowning, burning, or killing; this was mentioned by al-Farra'. According to the first view, *ajalin musamma* is an appointed term with Allah.

*(Inna ajala Allahi idha ja'a la yu'akhkhar)*: that is, when death comes it is not delayed, whether by punishment or without punishment. The term was attributed to Him, glorified is He, because He is the One who established it. It may also be attributed to people, as in His saying: ﴿So when their term comes﴾ [al-Nahl: 61], because it is set for them. *Law* here means *in* (if): that is, if you know. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: if you knew, you would know that the term of Allah, when it comes to you, is not delayed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 7:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, every time I call them﴾, that is, to the means of forgiveness, which is faith in You and obedience to You.

(They put their fingers in their ears) so that they would not hear my call (and covered themselves with their garments) meaning they covered their faces with them so that they would not see him. Ibn 'Abbas said: they placed their garments over their heads so that they would not hear his speech. So the covering with garments is then an addition to blocking the ears, so that they do not hear; or it is due to their rejecting themselves so that he would be silent; or so that they would make their turning away from him known to him. It was also said: it is a metaphor for enmity. It is said: "So-and-so put on for me the garments of enmity" (labisa li fulan thiyab al-'adawa).

(And they persisted) meaning in disbelief, so they did not repent.

(And they were arrogant) in refusing to accept the truth, because they said: ﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest of people follow you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 111].

(with great arrogance) — an emphasis (tafkhim).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 8–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed I invited them openly﴾, meaning, making the call manifest to them. It is in the accusative governed by "da'awtuhum" (I invited them) as an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), because calling out loud (al-jihar) is one of its two types. So it is put in the accusative by it, like "al-qurfusa'" (the squatting position) with "qa'ada" (sat), since it is one of the kinds of sitting. Or it is because he intended by "da'awtuhum" the meaning "jahartuhum" (I addressed them openly). It is also permissible for it to be an adjective of the verbal noun of "da'a," meaning an invitation that is "jihaaran," i.e., openly proclaimed. It may also be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: I invited them while openly addressing them with the call.

(Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking) meaning, I did not hold back any effort. Mujahid said: the meaning of "a'lantu" (I proclaimed) is "sihtu" (I cried out), and "asrartu lahum israran" (I spoke to them in private) means with the invitation, from one of them to another. It was also said: "asrartu lahum" means I came to them at their dwellings. All of this from Nuh, peace be upon him, is an exaggeration in calling them and gentleness in summoning them. The Haramiyyun (the Meccan and Medinan readers) and Abu 'Amr read the yā' in "innī a'lantu lahum" with a fatha (vowel), while the rest read it with sukun.

This passage contains three issues. The first concerns:

﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness﴾, i.e., ask Him for forgiveness of your past sins through sincere faith.

﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾. This is an encouragement to repentance. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Seeking forgiveness (al-istighfar) is an erasure of sins." Al-Fudayl said: "The servant says, 'I seek forgiveness from Allah,' and its interpretation is, 'Release me (aqilni).'"

The second concerns:

﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundance﴾, i.e., He will send down the water of the sky. There is an implied ellipsis here. It has also been said that "the sky" means rain, i.e., He will send down rain. The poet said:

"When the rain falls on the land of a people,
we graze there, even if they are angry."

The word "in abundance" (midrar) means with much rain. The verb "yursil" (He will send) is in the jussive because it is a response to the imperative.

Muqatil said: When they denied Noah for a long time, Allah withheld the rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for forty years. Their livestock and crops perished, so they came to Noah, peace be upon him, and sought his help. He said: ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾, meaning He has always been that for whoever turns to Him in repentance. Then, encouraging them to faith, he said: ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundance, and provide you with wealth and sons, and make for you gardens, and make for you rivers﴾. Qatadah said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) knew that they were people greedy for this world, so he said: "Come to obedience to Allah, for in obedience to Allah is the attainment of this world and the Hereafter."

The third concerns: this verse and the one in Surah Hud [see vol. 9, p. 51] are evidence that provision and rain can be drawn down through seeking forgiveness. Al-Sha'bi said: Umar went out to seek rain (istisqa'), and did nothing beyond seeking forgiveness until he returned. Then they were given rain, and they said: "We did not see you seek rain!" He said: "I sought rain with the majadih of the sky by which rain is drawn down." Then he recited: ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundance﴾.

[Ibn al-Athir said: "al-majadih" is the plural of majdah, with the yā' being extra for emphasis. Analogically its singular should be majdāh. The majdah is one of the stars, and among the Arabs it is one of the "anwā'" (star-risings) indicating rain. Seeking forgiveness was thus likened to the anwā' by addressing them in terms they understood, not as an affirmation of the anwā'. The plural form is used because he meant all the anwā' which they claim have the power to bring rain.]

Al-Awza'i said: The people went out to seek rain, and Bilal ibn Sa'd stood among them, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O Allah, we have heard You say: ﴿There is no path (of blame) against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91]. We have acknowledged our wrongdoing. Will Your forgiveness be only for those like us? O Allah, forgive us, have mercy on us, and give us water!" He raised his hands, and they raised their hands, and they were given water.

Ibn Subayh said: A man complained to al-Hasan about drought, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." Another complained to him about poverty, and he said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." Another said to him: "Pray to Allah that He grant me a son," and he said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." Another complained to him of the drying up of his garden, and he said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." We said to him about this, and he said: "I have said nothing from myself. Indeed Allah, the Exalted, says in the Surah of Noah: ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundance, and provide you with wealth and sons, and make for you gardens, and make for you rivers﴾."

The manner of seeking forgiveness has already been discussed in Surah Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 39], and that it is through sincerity and abandoning sins. And this is the basis of being answered.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verses 15–16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ He mentions to them another proof, meaning: Do you not know that the One who is able to do this is the One who must be worshipped? The meaning of ṭibāqan (in layers) is that some of them are above others, each heaven covering the other like domes. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi. Al-Hasan said: Allah created seven heavens in layers over seven earths, between each earth and earth, and heaven and heaven, is creation and command. His saying, "Have you not considered," is in the form of information, not of direct observation, as you say: "Have you not seen how I dealt with so-and-so?" Ṭibāqan is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "conforming in layers," or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) meaning "possessing layers," so that dhāt ("possessing") is omitted and ṭibāqan is put in its place.

﴿And made the moon therein a light﴾: meaning, in the lowest heaven, as one says: "The Banu Tamim came to me, and I went to the Banu Tamim," and what is meant is some of them. This is the view of al-Akhfash. Ibn Kaysan said: If it is in one of them, then it is in them all. Qutrub said: "fihinna" (in them) means "maʿahunna" (with them), and this is also the view of al-Kalbi, meaning that Allah created the sun and the moon along with the creation of the heavens and the earth. The majority of the linguists, regarding the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who was the most recent of his [[In the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays, p. 50, Hindiyya edition: "aḥdath" (most recent).]] covenant (ʿahd) enjoy, thirty months in three states?"

hold that fi means maʿa (with). Al-Nahhas said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Ibn Kaysan about this verse, and he said: The answer of the grammarians is that if he placed it in one of them, he has placed it in them all, as you say: "Give me the garments that are marked (muʿallama)," even though you only marked one of them. Another answer: It is related that the face of the moon is toward the heaven, and when it is toward its inside, it is connected to the heavens. The meaning of nūran (a light) is for the people of the earth; this is said by al-Suddi.

(Note) ʿAṭāʾ said: a light for the people of the heaven and the earth. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn ʿUmar said: its face shines on the people of the earth and its back shines on the people of the heaven.

﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾: meaning, a lamp for the people of the earth, so that they may reach their livelihoods through their activity. Concerning its shining on the people of the heaven, there are the two earlier opinions, as al-Mawardi related. Al-Qushayri related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the face of the sun is in the heavens and its back is on the earth. It was also said the reverse. It was said to ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar: What is the matter with the sun, that it scorches us at times and is cold to us at other times? He said: In summer it is in the fourth heaven, and in winter it is in the seventh heaven, near the Throne of the Most Merciful; and if it were in the lowest heaven, nothing would stand before it.

Nabatan (﴿نَبَاتاً﴾, "a growth") is a maṣdar (verbal noun, masdar) in a form other than the regular one, because its regular verbal noun is inbat (إِنْبَاتًا) from anbata. He complained to Allah, the Exalted, that they had disobeyed Him and had not followed Him in what He commanded them of faith. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, calling them while they remained upon their disbelief and rebellion.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Nuh, upon him be peace, hoped for the sons after the fathers, so they would bring forth children after children, until they reached seven generations (qurun). Then he invoked against them after despairing of them. He lived after the Flood sixty years, until the people multiplied and spread out.

al-Hasan said: The people of Nuh used to sow crops twice in a month. This was related by al-Mawardi.

"And they followed one whose wealth and children increased him only in loss" (﴿وَاتَّبَعُوا مَن لَّمْ يَزِدْهُ مَالُهُ وَوَلَدُهُ إِلَّا خَسَارًا﴾). He means their chiefs and their rich men, whose disbelief, wealth and children increased them only in misguidance in this world and destruction in the Hereafter.

The people of Madinah, Syria and 'Asim read "wa-waladuhu" (وَوَلَدُهُ) with a fatha on the waw and the lam. The rest read "wa-wulduhu" (وُلْدُهُ) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam, and this is a dialect form for "walad" (child). It is also permissible that it be a plural of "walad," like "al-fulk" (الفلك), which is both singular and plural. This has been discussed previously [see vol. 2, p. 194].

وَمَكَرُوا مَكْراً كُبَّاراً (22) — "and they schemed a great scheme." (Quran 71:22)

Ay, kabīran ʿaẓīman: great and mighty. It is said: kabīr, kubār and kubbār, like ʿajīb, ʿujāb and ʿujjāb, with the same meaning; and similarly ṭawīl, ṭuwāl and ṭuwwāl. It is said: rajul ḥasan and ḥussān, and jamīl and jummāl, and qurrāʾ for one who recites (al-qāriʾ), and wuḍḍāʾ for one who is very clean in wuḍūʾ (al-waḍīʾ).

Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

"A fair woman who hunts hearts and takes them captive, and with her glances the Muslim's heart is made a reciter (qurrāʾ)."

Another said:

"A man is joined to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, and not by being excessively clean (wuḍḍāʾ)."

Al-Mubarrad said: kubbāran (with shadda) is for emphasis (mubālaghah). Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ḥumayd and Mujāhid read kubāran (with no shadda).

It has been disputed what their scheme was. It was said: their inciting their lowly followers to kill Nuh. It was said: it is their deluding the people with what they were given of worldly goods and children, until the weak ones said: "Were they not upon the truth, they would not have been given these blessings." Al-Kalbi said: it is what they attributed to Allah of consorts and offspring. It was said: their scheme is their disbelief. Muqatil said: it is the saying of their great ones to their followers: "Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd, nor Suwaʿ, nor Yaghuth, nor Yaʿuq, nor Nasr."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 23–24:

Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: They were idols and images. The people of Noah worshipped them, and then the Arabs worshipped them. This is the view of the majority. It was also said: they belonged to the Arabs alone, and no one other than them worshipped them. They were the greatest of their idols and the most venerated among them, which is why they were singled out for mention after His saying, ﴿Do not leave your gods﴾. The meaning of the speech would then be as when the people of Noah said to their followers, "Do not leave your gods," and the Arabs said to their children and their people, "Do not leave Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, Ya'uq, or Nasr." Then the mention returned, after that, to the people of Noah, peace be upon him. According to the first view, the whole speech is in sequence concerning the people of Noah.

ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr and others said: Adam, peace be upon him, fell ill, and with him were his sons: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. Wadd was the eldest of them and the most dutiful to him. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: Adam, peace be upon him, had five sons: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. They were worshippers, and when one of them died they grieved over him. Satan said, "I will make an image of him for you; when you look at it you will remember him." They said, "Do it." So he made his image in the place of worship, of brass and lead. Then another died, and he made his image, until they all died and he made their images. Things declined as they decline today, until after a time they abandoned the worship of God, the Exalted. Satan said to them, "What is the matter with you that you do not worship anything?" They said, "And what should we worship?" He said, "Your gods and the gods of your fathers. Do you not see them in your places of prayer?" So they worshipped them besides God, until God sent Noah, and they said, ﴿Do not leave your gods, nor leave Wadd or Suwa'﴾, the verse.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb also said, and Muhammad ibn Qays: Rather, they were righteous people between Adam and Noah, and they had followers who emulated them. When they died, Iblis made it seem good to them that they should make images of their likenesses so that they would remember their striving through them, and so that they would find solace in looking at them. So he made their images. When they had died and others had come, they said, "Would that we knew! What did our fathers do with these images?" Then Satan came to them and said, "Your fathers used to worship them, and they would have mercy on you and give you rain." So they worshipped them, and the worship of idols began from that time.

I say: With this meaning has been explained what came in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of ʿA'ishah: that Umm Habibah and Umm Salamah mentioned a church they had seen in Abyssinia called Maria, in which there were images of the Messenger of God ﷺ.[[His saying "ra'aynaha" with the plural nun is because the least plural is two, or because there were other women with them. (al-Qastallani).]] The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Those people, when there was a righteous man among them and he died, they built a place of worship over his grave and made in it those images. Those are the worst of creation in the sight of God on the Day of Resurrection."[[His saying "to the Messenger of God ﷺ" is connected to "they mentioned to the Messenger of God ﷺ."]]

Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: These idols were names of righteous men from the people of Noah. When they perished, Satan inspired their people to set up, in the assemblies where they used to sit, standing stones, and to name them after them so that they would remember them by them. They did so, and they were not worshipped until those people had perished and knowledge had been effaced, and then they were worshipped besides God.

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that Noah, peace be upon him, used to guard the body of Adam, peace be upon him, on a mountain in India, preventing the disbelievers from circumambulating his grave. Satan said to them, "These people boast over you and claim that they are the sons of Adam to the exclusion of you, but it is only a body. I will make for you a likeness of it that you may circumambulate." So he fashioned for them these five idols and made them worship them. When the time of the Flood came, the clay, the dust and the water buried them, and they remained buried until Satan brought them out for the polytheists of the Arabs.

Al-Mawardi said: As for Wadd, it was the first idol worshipped. It was named Wadd because of their love (wudd) for it. After the people of Noah it belonged to the tribe of Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal, according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta' and Muqatil. And their poet said about it:

"May Wadd greet you, for it is not lawful for us
the play of women, and religion has resolved..."

As for Suwa', it belonged to Hudhayl on the sea coast, according to their view. As for Yaghuth, it belonged to Ghutayf of Murad in al-Jawf of Saba', according to the view of Qatadah. Al-Mahdawi said: It belonged to Murad and then to Ghatafan. Al-Tha'labi said: Ajaʾ and Antaʾ, both of Tayy, and the people of Jurash of Madhhij, took Yaghuth and carried it to Murad, and they worshipped it for a time. Then the Banu Najiyah wished to remove it from Ajaʾ and Antaʾ, so they fled with it to al-Husayn, brother of the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb of Khuza'ah. Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth, and it was of lead, and they used to carry it on a camel with a sprain (ahrad)[[al-Harad (with vowelization): a disease in the legs, so that when the camel walks it shakes its legs and strikes the ground with them often.]], and they would travel with it and not provoke it until it itself knelt down. When it knelt, they would alight and say, "It has approved the stopping place for you," and they would build a structure on it and alight around it.

As for Ya'uq, it belonged to Hamdan at Balkha'[[a place in Yemen]], according to the view of ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and ʿAta'. Al-Mawardi mentioned it. Al-Tha'labi said: As for Ya'uq, it belonged to Kahlan of Saba', then his sons inherited it, the eldest after the eldest,[[addition from the Tafsir of al-Tha'labi]] until it came to Hamdan. Concerning it Malik ibn Namat al-Hamdani said:

"God gives plumage in the world and makes it grow,
but Ya'uq does not make it grow, nor does it give plumage."

As for Nasr, it belonged to Dhu al-Kala' of Himyar, according to the view of Qatadah, and similarly from Muqatil. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 25:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ (*mimma khatī'ātihim ughriqū*). Here *mā* (ما) is a *ṣila* (a redundant, emphasizing particle), and the meaning is *min khaṭāyāhum* ("from their sins"). Al-Farra' said: the meaning is *min ajli khaṭāyāhum* ("because of their sins"), so *mā* carries this meaning. He said: *mā* indicates a conditional sense. [[Thus in the manuscripts of the original, and it is a reading.]]

The reading of Abu Amr is *khaṭāyāhum* (خَطَايَاهُمْ), in the broken plural (*jam' al-taksīr*), whose singular is *khaṭiyyah*. The original form of the plural was *khaṭā'iy* on the pattern *fa'ā'il*. When the two hamzas came together, the second was changed to a *yā'*, because it was preceded by a *kasra*, and then it was considered heavy, and the plural is heavy, and it is also defective (*mu'tall*). So the *yā'* was changed to an *alif*, and then the first hamza was changed to a *yā'* because it was hidden between the two *alifs*. The rest read *khaṭī'ātihim* (خَطِيئَاتِهِمْ) on the sound plural (*jam' al-salāmah*). Abu Amr said: "A people disbelieved for a thousand years, and they had only *khaṭiyyāt*," meaning that *khaṭāyā* is more numerous than *khaṭiyyāt*. Some people said: *khaṭāyā* and *khaṭiyyāt* are one, two plurals used both for many and for few, and they cited the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (Luqman: 27). The poet said: [[He is Hassan ibn Thabit.]]

*Lanā al-jafanāt al-ghurr yalma'na bi-l-ḍuḥā*
*wa-asyāfunā yaqṭarna min najdatin damā*

We have the white, shining platters that gleam in the forenoon,
and our swords that drip blood from the battle.

It is also read *khaṭī'ātihim* with the hamza changed to a *yā'* and assimilated (*idghām*). From al-Jahdari, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah and Ashhab al-'Uqayli it is reported as *khaṭī'atihim* (خَطِيئَتِهِمْ) in the singular, and the intended meaning is *shirk* (polytheism).

﴿Then they were made to enter a Fire﴾ (*fa-udkhilū nāran*), meaning after their drowning. Al-Qushayri said: this indicates the punishment of the grave. Those who deny it say: they became deserving of entering the Fire, or their places in the Fire were shown to them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ (Ghafir: 46). It was also said: they alluded to what is in the report about: "The sea is fire within fire." Abu Rawq narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿they were drowned, then made to enter a Fire﴾, he said: it means they were punished with fire in this world together with drowning in this world, in a single state; they were drowning on one side and burning in the water on the other side. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, who said: Abu al-Qasim al-Hubaybi recited to us, who said: Abu Sa'id Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Rumayh recited to us, who said: Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari recited to me:

*Al-khalqu mujtami'un ṭawran wa-muftariqun*
*wa-al-ḥādithātu funūnun dhātu aṭwār*

Creation is at times gathered and at times scattered,
and events are varied types with changing states.

*Lā ta'jabanna li-aḍdādin in ijtama'at*
*fa-Allāhu yajma'u bayna al-mā'i wa-al-nār*

Do not marvel at opposites when they come together,
for Allah joins water and fire.

﴿So they found for themselves, besides Allah, no helpers﴾ (*fa-lam yajidū lahum min dūni Allāhi anṣārā*), meaning: no one who would repel the punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 26–27:

In this matter there are four issues. The first: he (Nuh) prayed against them when he despaired of their following him. Qatadah said: he prayed against them after Allah had revealed to him: "Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed" [Hud: 36]. So Allah answered his supplication and drowned his people. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, Defeater of the confederates, defeat them and shake them." It was also said: the cause of his supplication was that a man from his people carried a small child on his shoulder and passed by Nuh, and he said: "Beware of this one, for he will mislead you." The child said: "O father, put me down," so he put him down, and the child threw him and wounded his head. At that point he became angry and prayed against them. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Muqatil, al-Rabi', Atiyyah and Ibn Zayd said: he said this when Allah had brought forth every believer from their loins and the wombs of their women. Allah rendered the wombs of the women and the loins of the men barren seventy years before the punishment. It was also said: forty years. Qatadah said: there were no children among them at the time of the punishment. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah said: had Allah destroyed their children along with them, that would have been a punishment from Allah upon them and justice concerning them; but Allah destroyed their children and offspring without punishment, then destroyed them with the punishment, based on the saying of the Exalted: "And the people of Nuh, when they denied the Messengers, We drowned them" [Al-Furqan: 37].

The second: Ibn al-Arabi said: "Nuh prayed against all the disbelievers, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed against those who banded together against the believers and incited against them. This is a basis for praying against disbelievers in general. As for a specific disbeliever whose end is not known, one does not pray against him, because his final state is unknown to us, and perhaps he is known to Allah to have a good end. The Prophet (ﷺ) specifically prayed against Utbah, Shaybah and their companions, because of his knowledge of their final state and what was revealed to him of their condition. And Allah knows best." I say: this issue has already been fully discussed in Surah al-Baqarah, and praise be to Allah.

The third: Ibn al-Arabi said: "If it is asked, why did Nuh make his supplication against his people a reason for his refraining from seeking intercession for creation from Allah on the Day of Judgment? We say: people have given two explanations for this. The first: that supplication arose from anger and harshness, whereas intercession comes from contentment and tenderness, so he feared being reproached and being told: 'You prayed against the disbelievers yesterday and you intercede for them today.' The second: that he prayed out of anger without a text or explicit permission for it, so he feared being held accountable for it on the Day of Resurrection, as Musa, peace be upon him, said: 'Indeed I killed a soul which I had not been commanded to kill.' He said: 'And this is what I say.'" I say: although he was not commanded to pray by explicit text, it was said to him: "Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed" [Hud: 36], so he was informed of their outcome and prayed for their destruction, just as our Prophet (ﷺ) prayed against Shaybah, Utbah and their likes, saying: "O Allah, deal with them," when he was informed of their outcome. On this view there is in it the meaning of a command to supplicate. And Allah knows best.

The fourth: the words of the Exalted: ﴿a dayyar. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except wicked disbelievers﴾, that is, one who dwells in the homes; this was said by al-Suddi. Its origin is daywar, on the pattern fay'al, from dar (to turn/dwell), so the waw was changed to ya' and one of the two was assimilated into the other, like al-qiyam, whose origin is qiywam. Had it been fa''al, it would have been dawwar. Al-Qutabi said: its origin is from al-dar, meaning one who settles in the dwelling; it is said: "There is no dayyar in the house," meaning no one. It was also said: al-dayyar is the owner of the house.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 71, verse 28:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. He supplicated for himself and for his parents, and both of them were believers. They were: Lamk (Lamak) son of Matushalakh (Mutushalakh), and Shamkha (Shamkhā) daughter of Anush. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri and al-Tha'labi. Al-Mawardi related that the name of his mother was Minjal.[[In the margin of al-Jamal: "Lamk" is with two fathas or with fatha followed by sukun. "Matushalakh" is with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the ta' and the waw, a sukun on the shin, and a kasra on the lam. "Shamkha" is on the pattern of "Sukra."]]

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: by "his parents" he meant his father and his grandfather. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also read "li-walidi" with a kasra on the dal, in the singular. Al-Kalbi said: between him and Adam there were ten fathers, all of whom were believers. Ibn 'Abbas said: no parent of Nuh (Noah) disbelieved between him and Adam, peace be upon them both.

﴿And for whoever enters my house as a believer﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 351.]], meaning my mosque and my place of prayer, praying and affirming belief in God. Only believers from among them would enter the houses of the prophets, so he made the mosque a cause for asking for forgiveness. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angels pray for one of you as long as he remains in the place where he prayed, as long as he does not break his wudu, saying: O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him," the hadith. It has already been mentioned. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: "my house" means my mosque; al-Tha'labi related it, and al-Dahhak said it. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: that is, "whoever enters my religion," so "house" means religion; al-Qushayri related it, and Juwaybir said it. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: he means my friend who enters my dwelling; al-Mawardi related it. It was also said: he meant my dar (home). It was said: my ship.

﴿And for the believing men and the believing women﴾ in general, until the Day of Resurrection; this was said by al-Dahhak. Al-Kalbi said: from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: from his people, and the first view is more apparent.

﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the disbelievers,

﴿except in ruin﴾, that is, except in destruction. So it is general for every disbeliever and polytheist. It was also said: he meant the polytheists of his people. Al-Tabar means destruction. It was also said: loss; al-Suddi related both meanings. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, these people—what they are engaged in will be destroyed﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 273.]] [al-A'raf: 139]. It was also said: al-tabar is annihilation, and the meaning is the same. And God knows best about this, and He is the One who grants success to what is correct.
